title: Software Requirements and Spec-Driven Development Frameworks

slides.title: What Are Software Requirements?
bullets: Definition: statements of what the system must do
Serve as contract between stakeholders and developers
Foundation for design, testing, and acceptance
slides.notes: Introduce the concept of requirements as the bridge between business needs and technical solutions. Emphasize that clear requirements reduce rework later.

slides.title: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
bullets: Functional: specific behaviors, inputs, outputs
Non-functional: performance, security, usability
Both must be captured for a complete specification
slides.notes: Explain the distinction with examples: a login function (functional) vs response time under 200 ms (non-functional). Mention that non-functional requirements often drive architecture decisions.

slides.title: Requirements Engineering Process
bullets: Elicitation – gather needs from stakeholders
Analysis – resolve conflicts, prioritize
Specification – document in a structured format
Validation – ensure requirements meet stakeholder intent
slides.notes: Walk through each phase, noting that iteration is common. Highlight that validation includes reviews, prototypes, and test case derivation.

slides.title: Use Cases and System Boundaries
bullets: Use case: a goal-oriented interaction between actor and system
System boundary defines what is inside vs outside the system
Actors can be humans, other systems, or devices
slides.notes: Show a simple context diagram. Stress that identifying the boundary early prevents scope creep. Relate to the spec-driven guideline of writing use cases before detailed specs.

slides.title: Deriving Use Cases from a Product Description
bullets: Product: online refund request portal
Actors: Customer, Support Agent, Payment Gateway
Use cases: Submit Request, Review Request, Process Refund, Notify Customer
slides.notes: Demonstrate how to read a narrative and extract actors and use cases. This directly supports LO1 (outline use cases from unstructured descriptions).

slides.title: Check: Classifying Requirements

quiz.question: Which of the following is a non-functional requirement for the refund portal?
options: The system shall allow a customer to submit a refund request.
The system shall process refunds within 2 business days.
The system shall send an email notification after refund approval.
The system shall integrate with the existing payment gateway.
quiz.explanation: Option B describes a performance constraint (time bound), which is a non-functional requirement. Option A, C, and D describe specific system behaviors (functional).

slides.notes: Quick in-class poll. Discuss why performance, security, and usability are non-functional.

slides.title: Writing Good Requirements (SMART & IEEE 830)
bullets: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound
Unambiguous, testable, traceable
Use consistent terminology and structure
slides.notes: Present a before/after example: vague vs SMART requirement. Mention IEEE 830 as a standard template for requirement specifications.

slides.title: Traceability and Validation
bullets: Trace each requirement to design, code, and test artifacts
Bidirectional traceability supports impact analysis
Validation techniques: reviews, prototypes, acceptance tests
slides.notes: Explain how traceability matrices are built and used during change management. Connect to later spec-driven development where executable specs serve as living traceability artifacts.

slides.title: Part 1 Recap: Requirements Engineering Essentials
bullets: Requirements define what the system must do
Functional and non-functional types
Process: elicitation → analysis → specification → validation
Use cases capture actor–system interactions
Good requirements are SMART and traceable
slides.notes: Briefly recap the first 60 minutes. Ask if any concepts need clarification before moving to spec-driven frameworks.

slides.title: Spec-Driven Development Overview
bullets: Specifications written in executable form drive implementation
Reduces gap between requirements and code
Enables automated test generation and verification
slides.notes: Introduce the paradigm shift: specs become first-class artifacts. Cite the 2026 paper on specification-driven development as a structured approach for source code generation.

slides.title: Executable Specifications: Definition and Benefits
bullets: Executable spec = formal, machine-readable description of behavior
Can be run as tests before any implementation exists
Supports continuous validation and living documentation
slides.notes: Contrast with traditional textual specs. Mention tools like Gherkin, SpecFlow, or Python's pytest-bdd. Highlight that executable specs meet the interface specification for every public method (LO2).

slides.title: Worked Example: Executable Spec for Refund Processing
bullets: Define the public interface: process_refund(request_id, amount)
Write a spec that asserts expected outcomes
Provide a minimal implementation to make the spec pass

figure.caption: Executable specification and stub implementation in Python

slides.notes: Walk through the code line by line. Explain that the spec (test) is written first, then the stub makes it pass. In practice, the spec would be more detailed and the implementation generated or written to satisfy it. This demonstrates translating module requirements into executable specifications (LO2).

slides.title: Check: Characteristics of Executable Specifications

quiz.question: What is a key benefit of executable specifications over traditional textual specs?
options: They are easier to write for non-technical stakeholders.
They can be automatically executed to validate behavior.
They eliminate the need for any testing.
They replace the need for version control.
quiz.explanation: Executable specifications can be run as automated tests, providing continuous validation. Option A is false because they often require technical syntax. Option C is false; they complement but do not replace testing. Option D is unrelated.

slides.notes: In-class quiz to reinforce the definition and value of executable specs.

slides.title: From Executable Specs to Code Generation
bullets: Specs define contracts for each public method
Code generators can scaffold implementations from specs
Human developers fill in business logic, preserving spec compliance
slides.notes: Describe the workflow: write spec, run generator to produce interface stubs, developers implement bodies. Mention that this aligns with the course's later lab on executable specification and code generation.

slides.title: Lecture Summary: Requirements to Executable Specs
bullets: Requirements engineering provides the foundation
Use cases capture system boundaries and actor goals
Spec-driven development turns requirements into executable specifications
Executable specs serve as living documentation and automated tests
Next steps: lab on writing and running executable specs
slides.notes: Conclude the 90-minute session. Highlight the two learning outcomes achieved. Remind students of upcoming lab and assignments.
